title: El Nino Is Here. India's Monsoon Season Faces Its Biggest Threat in a Decade.
excerpt: U.S. and Indian forecasters have confirmed El Nino conditions that could slash rainfall, shrink harvests, and push food prices higher as 200 million rain-fed farming households begin sowing.
body:
India's monsoon season officially began on June 1, but the outlook for the next four months just got considerably darker. Both the U.S. Climate Prediction Center and the India Meteorological Department have confirmed that El Nino conditions are now present in the tropical Pacific — and are expected to strengthen into a moderate-to-strong event by winter.

For India, where the June-to-September monsoon delivers nearly 70 per cent of annual rainfall and sustains an agricultural sector worth 18 per cent of the country's $4 trillion economy, the implications are enormous. IMD now projects cumulative monsoon rainfall at roughly 90 per cent of the long-period average of 870 millimetres — a polite way of saying the country is heading into a below-normal rain year.

## The Pattern Is Familiar. The Stakes Are Not.

El Nino is not new to India. The last strong event, in 2015-16, brought drought to large parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana, and forced New Delhi to draw down grain buffer stocks and restrict rice exports. But the 2026 edition arrives in a more fragile context.

The Strait of Hormuz blockade drove up fertiliser costs for months. Global supply chains for urea and diammonium phosphate — India's two most consumed fertilisers — were disrupted when the war pushed freight insurance premiums to wartime levels. Although the U.S.-Iran deal announced on Sunday should ease shipping costs, Indian warehouses have been drawing down stocks through the kharif sowing window.

Meanwhile, climate scientists are warning this event could intensify further. "The current forecasts have El Nino strengthening to over 2 degrees Celsius, which is a very strong event if it pans out," said Dartmouth's Daniel Mankin. "In absolute dollar terms, this could be the costliest El Nino on record."

## What Gets Hit First

The immediate risk falls on kharif crops — rice, cotton, soybeans, pulses, and sugarcane — which depend on monsoon rains for planting and early growth. IMD expects early June rainfall to hold relatively steady, but August and September are likely to bear the brunt of El Nino's suppressive effect on the Indian Ocean moisture corridor.

Rice is the headline concern. India is the world's largest rice exporter, and any significant production shortfall tends to trigger export restrictions. In 2023, New Delhi banned non-basmati white rice exports and imposed duties on parboiled rice when a weaker El Nino dented output. A stronger event this year could prompt similar moves, rippling through global food markets.

Pulses and oilseeds — already facing chronic supply-demand imbalances in India — are equally vulnerable. The Hindu Business Line reported that vegetable prices are likely to spike first, given shorter production cycles and the limited shelf life of tomatoes, onions, and leafy greens.

## The Inflation Calculus

The Reserve Bank of India cut its policy rate to 6 per cent in April and signalled further easing as headline inflation eased below 4 per cent. But a weak monsoon could reverse that trajectory. Food accounts for nearly 46 per cent of India's consumer price index basket, and any sustained spike in vegetable and cereal prices feeds directly into headline inflation.

Outlook Business warned that if production of pulses, oilseeds, and coarse cereals declines, "retail prices could rise, adding pressure to household budgets" and complicating the RBI's efforts to keep inflation within its target range. Higher food prices would also constrain the central bank's room to cut rates further — exactly when the economy needs monetary support to sustain its 6.5 per cent growth trajectory.

The government has some tools: releasing grain from the 60-million-tonne buffer stock maintained by the Food Corporation of India, increasing import quotas, and restricting exports. But each of these carries trade-offs. Export bans anger trading partners and hurt farmers' incomes. Import surges strain foreign exchange reserves. Buffer drawdowns work only if the reserves were adequately built — and procurement has been patchy in recent years.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRI families with roots in agricultural states — Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu — the monsoon is not an abstraction. It determines whether relatives in smaller towns and villages face stable prices or sudden inflation in staples like dal, rice, and cooking oil.

Remittance corridors are already under strain. The rupee's recent slide to 95 per dollar, driven by the Hormuz crisis, made dollar transfers more valuable in rupee terms — but the underlying need was growing. Higher food prices in India could increase remittance demand from households that depend on overseas earnings to supplement farm income.

There is also a property and investment angle. Weak monsoons historically dampen rural consumption, which accounts for roughly 35 per cent of India's GDP. That softness tends to show up in corporate earnings for consumer goods, two-wheelers, and rural lending — all sectors where NRI investors hold significant exposure through mutual funds and direct equity.

## What to Watch

The next four weeks will be decisive. Sowing progress in July — tracked weekly by the Agriculture Ministry — will show whether farmers are planting at normal rates or holding back in anticipation of poor rains. The IMD's monthly bulletin, due in early July, will update its El Nino intensity forecast. And the government's first advance estimate of kharif production, expected in September, will set the tone for food policy through the winter.

India has survived El Nino before. But this time, the margin for error is thinner, the global supply chains are more fragile, and the fiscal cushion is smaller. For the 200 million households that still look to the sky each June, the next monsoon is not just a weather event. It is the year's biggest economic variable.
